title: Daily Devotionals
subtitle: Short readings for an ordinary morning
blurb: Short devotional readings — a passage, a thought, and a prayer — for the ordinary mornings that make up most of a life with God.

chapters.title: How to Read the Bible Devotionally
chapters.summary: Most people who quit reading the Bible quit because they were taught to read it the way they read everything else, fast and for information, and the oldest tradition of Christian reading is built on the exact opposite instinct.
chapters.body:
I came to the Bible the way a former atheist comes to anything, to master it. I read it to find the contradictions, then, after I believed, I read it to find the arguments, the doctrines, the proof texts I could deploy. I read it fast, the way I read everything, mining it for information I could carry out and use. And for a long time I could not understand why a book I now believed was the word of God left me so unchanged. I was reading it correctly by every standard I knew. The standards were the problem.

There is a way of reading the Bible that gathers information, and it is good and necessary and the church needs more of it, not less. But there is an older way, nearly lost, that the tradition called reading for formation rather than information, reading not to get something out of the text but to let the text get something out of you. And almost no one teaches it anymore, because almost everything in our world trains us in the opposite direction. We read to extract. We skim, we scan, we pull the takeaway and move on. Bring that habit to Scripture and you will treat the living word like a feed to be consumed, and you will get exactly what you get from a feed. Nothing that stays.

Let me give the strongest case for the other approach, the study-first approach, because I hold it too and I do not want to caricature it. The serious reader says the Bible is an ancient text in foreign languages from cultures three thousand years gone, and to read it devotionally without first reading it carefully is to read your own reflection back to yourself. You will make it say whatever you already feel. Better to learn the history, the grammar, the context, to understand what the author meant before you ask what it means for you, or you will turn the Bible into a mirror and call your reflection God. This is true. I have watched devotional reading become exactly that, a warm fog in which people find divine endorsement of whatever they already wanted. The guardrail of careful study is not optional, and I am not arguing against it.

But here is what careful study cannot do by itself, and what the study-only reader sometimes forgets. You can understand a text completely and remain untouched by it. Knowledge of Scripture is not the same as formation by Scripture, and the most informed reader in the room can be the least changed. Jesus said this to the most expert Bible readers of his day. You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life, and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me (John 5:39-40 ESV). They had the text mastered. They had memorized it. And they walked straight past the One it was pointing to, because they were reading for information about God and never let it become an encounter with him. That is the warning hanging over every careful reader, myself most of all. You can win the argument about the text and lose the thing the text was for.

Hold that text as the spine. The Scriptures bear witness, they point, they are not the destination but the finger pointing at the destination. Read for information and you stop at the finger. Read devotionally and you follow it to the face.

The history here is encouraging, because the way of reading we have lost was the normal way for most of Christian history. The monastic tradition formalized it under a Latin name, lectio divina, sacred reading, and it had four slow movements that ran exactly counter to how we read now. You read the text slowly, lectio. You stopped on the word or phrase that arrested you and turned it over, meditatio. You let it become prayer, oratio. And you fell silent and let God act, contemplatio. The whole thing assumed that the point of reading was not coverage but encounter, not how many chapters but whether you met God in one verse. Eugene Peterson recovered this for the modern church and gave it a memorable image, that we are to read Scripture the way a dog works a bone, not racing through it but staying with it, gnawing, returning, getting the marrow out, what the old writers called rumination (Peterson 2006). We have become readers who swallow whole and digest nothing.

Then the printing press changed how everyone reads, and Scripture got swept up in it. After Gutenberg in the 1450s, and far more after mass literacy, reading became fast, silent, private, and extractive, a tool for gathering information at speed. That was a gift to the world and to the spread of the Bible itself. But a side effect was that the slow, communal, ruminative reading that had formed Christians for a thousand years came to feel inefficient, even strange. And then the screen finished what the press began. The smartphone, arriving in 2007, trained us to read in fragments, to scan for the relevant line and bounce away, attention shattered into seconds. Bring that shattered attention to the Psalms and you will get nothing, not because the Psalms have failed but because you are reading a deep thing with a shallow instrument. We do not have a Bible problem. We have an attention problem, and it follows us onto the page.

So how do you read devotionally. Slowly, and three small turns make the difference, because the practice really does have three. Read less and stay longer. Read it as addressed to you. And let it become prayer.

Read less and stay longer. Abandon the chapters-per-day arithmetic. Take five verses, or one. Read them three times, the third time aloud, because the ear catches what the racing eye skips. Stop on the word that snags you and stay there until it gives something up. You are not trying to cover the Bible. You are trying to let one true sentence go all the way down.

Read it as addressed to you. Not as a document about ancient people but as a letter that has reached its recipient. When the text says fear not, hear it spoken to you, in your kitchen, on the Tuesday you are afraid. This is where the study guardrail matters, so that you receive what the text actually says and not what you wish it said, but once you understand it rightly, you must let it speak to you and not only to the Israelites. The word is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword, and it discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart (Hebrews 4:12 ESV). A sword you study on a shelf cuts nothing. Let it be drawn.

Let it become prayer. The moment a verse opens, stop reading and start praying it back. If the text says the Lord is my shepherd, pray it, tell him you have wandered, ask him to lead you. The reading was always meant to turn into conversation. That turn, from reading about God to speaking with God, is the whole hinge of devotional reading, and the page is just where the conversation starts.

The law and the grace are both in this practice, and the law comes first as it always does. When you slow down and let the word actually read you, it will expose you. The verse you stayed with will name the thing in you that you were reading fast to avoid. That is the sword doing its work, and it will hurt, and it is supposed to. But the One the Scriptures bear witness to did not come to leave you cut open. He came to heal the thing the word exposed. The whole canon is a finger pointing at a cross, and the cross is where the indictment the text raises against you is answered, fully, by him, in your place. Augustine was undone not by mastering Scripture but by a single sentence of it read at the right moment in a garden, take up and read, and he took it up, and it read him, and he was never the same (Augustine 397). That is devotional reading. Not information carried out. A self handed over.

Stop trying to get through the Bible. Let one verse get through to you. That is the whole of it, and most of us have never once done it.

### Works Cited

Augustine. 397. Confessions. Translated by Henry Chadwick. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991.

Peterson, Eugene H. 2006. Eat This Book: A Conversation in the Art of Spiritual Reading. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

chapters.title: How to Talk About Faith Without Being Weird
chapters.summary: Most Christians have been trained to share their faith in ways that guarantee nobody wants to hear it. The problem is not the gospel. The problem is us.
chapters.body:
There is a reason people change the subject when a Christian starts talking about faith. It is not because the culture has become hostile to spiritual conversation. It is not because secularism has closed every ear. It is because Christians, by and large, have earned the awkwardness. We have been trained in methods of evangelism that treat human beings as targets, conversations as opportunities, and relationships as means to an end. And people can feel it. They have always been able to feel it.

The history of modern evangelism is, in many ways, a history of industrialization applied to the soul. In 1962, D. James Kennedy developed Evangelism Explosion, a program that reduced the gospel presentation to a scripted conversation beginning with two diagnostic questions: "Have you come to a place in your spiritual life where you know for certain that if you were to die today you would go to heaven?" and "Suppose that you were to die tonight and stand before God and He were to say to you, 'Why should I let you into my heaven?' What would you say?" The program trained millions. It also taught an entire generation that sharing faith meant executing a script on an unsuspecting person, ideally steering them to a decision within a single conversation.

Bill Bright's Four Spiritual Laws, published in 1965, compressed the gospel into a pocket-sized booklet that could be walked through in under five minutes. Campus Crusade for Christ distributed over 2.5 billion copies worldwide. The method was efficient, reproducible, and almost entirely devoid of the one thing that makes spiritual conversation meaningful: actual relationship with the person you are talking to.

These methods were not invented by cynical people. They were developed by men and women who genuinely believed that eternity hung in the balance and that efficiency in gospel proclamation was a moral imperative. But the unintended consequence was the creation of an entire culture of faith-sharing built on the assumption that evangelism is something you do to people rather than something that happens between people. And the damage has been enormous.

Why It Feels Wrong

The discomfort people feel when a Christian steers a conversation toward faith is not irrational. It is the entirely rational response to being instrumentalized. When someone realizes that a friendship, a conversation, or even a kind act has been undertaken with the ulterior motive of converting them, the feeling is not gratitude. It is betrayal. The relationship was not real. It was bait.

The sociologist Christian Smith has documented what he calls the "personal influence strategy" in American evangelicalism — the deliberate cultivation of relationships for the purpose of evangelism. Small groups are organized around it. Church planting strategies depend on it. "Friendship evangelism," the softer alternative to cold-contact methods, still carries the fundamental problem: the friendship is a means, not an end. And human beings, who have evolved over millennia to detect social deception, can sense the difference between someone who is genuinely interested in them and someone who is interested in their conversion.

The culture war posture of the last forty years has compounded the problem. When Christianity became publicly associated with partisan politics, moral condemnation, and opposition to the rights of marginalized groups, the word "Christian" itself became a liability in conversation. To announce oneself as a Christian in a secular workplace or social setting is now, for many hearers, to announce a set of political commitments that have nothing to do with Jesus of Nazareth and everything to do with a movement that has used his name for purposes he would not recognize. The person across the table does not hear "I follow a first-century rabbi who taught enemy-love and died for it." They hear "I am part of the group that wants to control your body, your bedroom, and your ballot." Whether that perception is fair is beside the point. It is the reality in which we operate.

The Art of Earned Conversation

The New Testament word for witness is martys, from which we get the English word "martyr." This is not a coincidence. In the early church, witness was not a technique. It was a life — a life so visibly different, so marked by sacrificial love, generosity, and courage, that people asked questions. The earliest Christians did not have evangelism programs. They had a community that shared possessions, welcomed strangers, cared for the sick during plagues when everyone else fled, and buried the dead that other communities abandoned. And people noticed.

The first principle of talking about faith without being weird is earning the conversation. This means that faith comes up because your life has provoked a genuine question, not because you have manufactured an opening. It means that the person you are talking to has seen something in your life — your patience under pressure, your generosity without strings, your willingness to sit with someone in grief without offering platitudes — that has made them curious. The conversation is pulled from you, not pushed onto them.

This requires a fundamental shift in posture. Instead of looking for opportunities to insert the gospel into conversations, you live in such a way that the gospel inserts itself. Instead of preparing answers to questions nobody has asked, you become the kind of person whose life raises questions that people actually want answered.

Peter's instruction in his first letter is more psychologically sophisticated than most evangelism training: "Always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that you have. But do this with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:15). Notice the sequence. Someone asks. You answer. You do it gently. The entire weight of the passage falls on the assumption that your life has already done the work of provoking the question.

Language That Works

The language of the church is a foreign language in secular spaces, and Christians who use it without translation are not being faithful. They are being lazy. Words like "saved," "washed in the blood," "born again," "convicted by the Spirit," "called," and "anointed" carry rich theological meaning within the Christian tradition. Outside of it, they sound like the vocabulary of a cult.

This is not a modern problem. Paul modeled the principle of linguistic adaptation in his address at the Areopagus in Acts 17. Speaking to Greek philosophers, he did not quote Torah. He quoted their own poets — Epimenides and Aratus. He began with what they already knew and valued, built bridges from their existing categories, and introduced the distinctive claims of the gospel only after establishing common ground. He did not water down his message. He translated it.

In practice, this means describing your experience of faith in ordinary human language. Instead of "God convicted me of my sin," you might say, "I came to a point where I had to be honest about the ways I was hurting people I loved." Instead of "I was saved," you might say, "Something shifted in me — I stopped trying to earn my way into being acceptable, and I started trusting that I already was." Instead of "I feel called to ministry," you might say, "I realized that the work that mattered most to me was helping people find their way through the hardest parts of their lives."

This is not compromise. It is communication. The substance is identical. The packaging respects the listener enough to meet them where they actually are rather than where you wish they were.

Listening as the First Act of Witness

The most underrated evangelistic skill is one that appears in almost no evangelism training manual: the capacity to listen. Not to listen for an opening. Not to listen while preparing your response. But to listen with genuine curiosity about another person's experience, convictions, and questions — to listen in such a way that the other person feels heard, not managed.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote in Life Together that "the first service that one owes to others in the fellowship consists in listening to them. Just as love to God begins with listening to His Word, so the beginning of love for the brethren is learning to listen to them." He went further: "He who can no longer listen to his brother will soon be no longer listening to God either; he will be doing nothing but prattle in the presence of God too."

When someone tells you they do not believe in God, the faithful response is not to argue. It is to ask what they mean by "God" — because in many cases, the God they do not believe in is one you should not believe in either. The bearded man in the sky dispensing rewards and punishments. The cosmic vending machine who grants wishes to the sufficiently pious. The tribal deity who blesses one nation and curses another. These are gods worth rejecting. And the person who has rejected them may be closer to the true God than the person who has never questioned the caricature.

When someone tells you they left the church, the faithful response is not to defend the church. It is to ask what happened. And then to listen. And if what they describe is abuse, manipulation, judgment, or hypocrisy — to say, simply, "I am sorry. That should not have happened to you." Not "but not all churches are like that." Not "you should try my church." Just the acknowledgment that what happened to them was wrong. That acknowledgment, offered without agenda, is more powerful than any gospel presentation ever devised.

When to Speak and When to Be Silent

The wisdom tradition of Scripture is emphatic about the relationship between speech and silence. "Even fools are thought wise if they keep silent, and discerning if they hold their tongues" (Proverbs 17:28). Ecclesiastes names "a time to be silent and a time to speak" (3:7). James warns that "everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak" (1:19). The weight of biblical counsel falls heavily on the side of restraint.

Speak when someone has asked a genuine question and is waiting for a genuine answer. Speak when your silence would be a form of cowardice — when someone is being harmed and your faith compels you to say so. Speak when you have earned enough trust that your words will be received as coming from someone who cares, not someone who is performing.

Be silent when the other person is processing grief. Be silent when you have not been asked. Be silent when speaking would be more about your need to be right than their need to be heard. Be silent when the situation calls for presence, not proclamation.

The most powerful witness I have ever seen was a man who sat with a grieving neighbor for three hours without saying a word about God. He brought food. He sat. He listened. He came back the next day and did the same thing. Six months later, that neighbor asked him why he had come. "Because that is what I believe love looks like," he said. The neighbor started coming to church the following week. No script. No strategy. Just a life that made someone curious about its source.

There is a practical dimension to this that deserves to be stated plainly. The Christian who learns to talk about faith without being weird is the Christian who has internalized a set of social skills that the church has historically failed to teach: reading the room, respecting boundaries, distinguishing between a genuine invitation to speak and a polite silence that is being mistaken for one. These are not spiritual gifts. They are social competencies, and they can be learned. The person who cannot tell the difference between a coworker's genuine curiosity about their weekend church service and a coworker's polite attempt to end the conversation is not lacking in the Spirit. They are lacking in social awareness, and the two should not be confused.

The Apostle Paul, who was many things, was also a remarkably perceptive reader of social contexts. He adjusted his approach depending on his audience — Jews in the synagogue, Greeks in the marketplace, Romans in the courtroom. He did not change his message. He changed his method. He understood that communication is not merely about the content of what you say but about the context in which you say it, the relationship you have with the person you are saying it to, and the cultural codes that govern how speech is received. Christians who ignore these factors in the name of faithfulness are not being faithful. They are being socially incompetent and baptizing their incompetence with theology.

The gospel does not need our salesmanship. It needs our lives. It needs communities so marked by love that people cannot explain them by any ordinary social theory. It needs individuals so formed by grace that their patience, generosity, and honesty provoke the question that no evangelism program can manufacture: "What is different about you?"

That question, when it comes, is holy ground. Answer it honestly, gently, and briefly. Then stop talking. Let the silence do its work. The Spirit has been in this conversation longer than you have.

chapters.title: Jubilee Economics Today
chapters.summary: The ancient law of jubilee mandated a periodic reset of land, debt, and freedom. It has been dismissed as an impractical relic — but the impulse behind it may be the most urgent economic word the church has to offer.
chapters.body:
Buried in Leviticus 25, in a book most Christians never read, sits one of the most radical economic ideas in human history. Every fifty years, the law commanded, Israel was to sound the trumpet and proclaim liberty throughout the land. Debts would be cancelled. Slaves would go free. And most astonishingly, all ancestral land that had been sold or lost over the preceding half-century would return, without payment, to the families who had originally held it. The whole economic order would be reset. The accumulation of wealth and the accumulation of poverty that had built up over two generations would be dissolved in a single year, and the nation would start again from something closer to equality.

This is the jubilee, and modern readers do not know what to do with it. It is routinely dismissed as impractical, utopian, perhaps never even fully implemented, a curious relic of an ancient agrarian society with no bearing on modern economic life. And it is true that jubilee, taken as a literal legal prescription, does not transfer to a modern industrial economy. But to dismiss it on those grounds is to miss the point entirely. The jubilee was never merely a piece of legislation. It was a theological declaration about the nature of ownership, the danger of permanent inequality, and the God who refuses to let the poor stay poor forever. And that declaration may be exactly what the church most needs to recover.

The Land Is Mine

The jubilee is grounded in a single sentence that undermines the entire modern conception of property. "The land is mine," God says, "and you reside in my land as foreigners and strangers." This is the theological foundation, and it is worth sitting with, because it contradicts an assumption so basic we never examine it: that what we own, we own absolutely. In the biblical vision, no human being ever owns land absolutely. God owns it. Human beings are tenants, stewards, temporary holders of what ultimately belongs to another. The land could not be sold permanently, because it was never truly the seller's to sell. At most, one could sell the use of the land until the next jubilee, when it reverted to its true owner's arrangement.

This reframes ownership entirely. If God owns everything and we are tenants, then our property rights are real but limited, held under an authority that has its own claims and purposes. The jubilee was the periodic enforcement of God's ultimate ownership against the human tendency to treat possession as absolute. It said, in effect: you may hold this for a time, but you do not own it forever, and the God who does own it has decreed that it will not remain permanently concentrated in the hands of the few while the many are dispossessed. Ownership is stewardship under a Lord who cares how the resources of his land are distributed.

The jubilee rests on four words that dismantle our whole economics: the land is mine. You do not own it forever. You hold it, as a tenant, under an owner who will not let the poor stay poor.

The Problem Jubilee Addresses

To understand why jubilee matters, you have to understand the problem it was designed to solve, and it is a problem no economy has ever escaped. Over time, wealth concentrates. The able and the fortunate and the ruthless accumulate more; the unlucky and the vulnerable fall behind; debt loads the poor and dispossesses them; and generation by generation the gap widens until a small elite holds most of the resources and a large underclass holds almost nothing. This is not a bug in fallen economies. It is their default trajectory. Left alone, every economy drifts toward oligarchy, with wealth and land and power pooling at the top and hardening into permanence.

The jubilee was God's structural interruption of this drift. It did not prevent inequality from developing over the decades — people would still rise and fall, gain and lose, within the fifty-year cycle. But it prevented inequality from becoming permanent and hereditary. Every fifty years, the drift was reversed. The family that had lost everything got its inheritance back. The debt that had accumulated was cancelled. No family could be permanently locked into poverty, and no family could permanently monopolize the land. The jubilee built a limit into the system — a horizon beyond which dispossession could not extend, a guarantee that poverty would not become a life sentence passed down to the children and the children's children.

Jesus and the Jubilee

The jubilee is not left behind in the Old Testament. When Jesus stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth to announce his ministry, he read from Isaiah 61: "The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim freedom for the prisoners and recovery of sight for the blind, to set the oppressed free, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor." That last phrase — the year of the Lord's favor — is jubilee language. Isaiah was drawing on the imagery of the jubilee year, and Jesus was applying it to himself. He was announcing that his ministry was the true jubilee, the great release, the year of the Lord's favor come in person.

What Jesus did with the jubilee is instructive. He did not enact it as national legislation; he was not a political reformer in that sense. But he took its meaning — release, freedom, good news to the poor, the reversal of the accumulated weight of debt and bondage — and made it the center of his mission. The kingdom he proclaimed was a jubilee kingdom, one in which debts are forgiven, the poor are lifted, the captives are freed, and the accumulated injustices of the world are being undone. The Lord's Prayer itself carries the jubilee impulse: forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors. The jubilee did not disappear. It was transfigured and placed at the heart of the gospel.

What It Asks of Us Now

So what does jubilee economics ask of the church today? Not, I think, a legislative program that any congregation could adopt, and not a naive attempt to reimpose Mosaic land law on a modern nation. But it asks for something, and the something is real. It asks us to hold our own property as tenants rather than absolute owners, knowing that God owns it and has purposes for it beyond our comfort. It asks us to be a people of forgiveness in the economic sense — releasing what is owed to us, refusing to demand the last ounce, practicing in our own dealings the release the jubilee proclaimed. It asks us to care intensely about whether the poor in our reach are locked into permanent poverty, and to work against that entrenchment wherever we can.

And it asks the church, perhaps most pointedly, to be an outpost of jubilee in a world that runs on its opposite. Where the world accumulates, the church releases. Where the world lets inequality harden, the church works to reverse it. Where the world treats ownership as absolute, the church treats everything as held in trust from the God who owns it all. The church that forgives debts — literal and relational — that lifts the fallen, that refuses to let poverty become permanent among its people, that shares its resources so that no one among it is in serious need, is enacting the jubilee in miniature. This is not utopian. It is precisely what the early church in Acts did when they shared their possessions so that there was no needy person among them. That was jubilee, embodied in a community.

The Trumpet We Have Silenced

I suspect the reason we have dismissed the jubilee as impractical is not primarily that it is impractical. It is that it is inconvenient. Jubilee threatens the accumulation that most of us, myself included, are quietly organizing our lives around. It is easier to declare it a relic than to let it interrogate our own grip on what we hold. The trumpet that was meant to sound liberty across the land has been silenced, not because it could not be sounded, but because we would rather not hear what it says about our debts and our dispossessions and our absolute ownership of things that were never truly ours.

Why the First Sermon Was a Jubilee

It is worth pausing on the fact that Jesus chose the jubilee for his inaugural announcement, because the choice was not accidental and its implications are enormous. Of all the texts he could have read to launch his public ministry, of all the ways he could have summarized what he came to do, he selected the passage that proclaims the year of the Lord's favor — release for captives, sight for the blind, freedom for the oppressed, good news for the poor. He defined his entire mission in the vocabulary of the jubilee, and then he sat down and said, today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.

This means the gospel is, at its heart, a jubilee gospel. The salvation Jesus brings is release — release from the debt of sin, release from the bondage of the law of sin and death, release from every accumulated weight that the fall has piled on the human race. And it means the community that receives this gospel cannot be indifferent to the economic release the jubilee also proclaimed, because the spiritual release and the material release flow from the same heart of God and cannot finally be separated. A church that preaches release from spiritual debt while ignoring the economic bondage of the poor at its gate has torn apart what Jesus held together in a single sermon. The jubilee gospel liberates the whole person, and it forms a people who long to see liberation extend into every corner of a bound and burdened world.

The Practice of Release

How does a community actually live jubilee in an economy structured entirely against it? Not by waiting for the legislation that will never come, but by becoming, in its own life, a colony of the coming kingdom where the jubilee logic already operates. It begins small and concrete: forgiving actual debts owed to us when we are able, refusing to demand the last dollar from someone drowning, structuring our generosity so that the accumulated weight on the poor among us is genuinely lifted rather than merely acknowledged.

It extends to how we hold our own resources — as tenants rather than absolute owners, ready to release what God directs us to release, unwilling to let our wealth become the permanent fortress the jubilee was designed to prevent. And it extends to the character of our common life, a community where, as in Acts, the sharing is real enough that there is no destitute person left unhelped in the fellowship. None of this reforms the national economy. All of it makes the church a living sign of the jubilee it proclaims, a foretaste of the great release, a people who have heard the trumpet and begun, however imperfectly, to live as though the year of the Lord's favor had actually arrived.

The Objection of the Prudent

The immediate objection to jubilee economics comes from the prudent, and it deserves a hearing rather than a dismissal. If debts are cancelled every seven years and land returns every fifty, the objector asks, who would ever lend, and who would work hard to acquire what they cannot permanently keep? Does jubilee not punish diligence and reward improvidence, dissolving the incentives that make an economy function at all? It is a serious question, and the law itself anticipated it. Deuteronomy explicitly warns against the hard-hearted person who refuses to lend as the year of release approaches, calculating that the debt will soon be cancelled, and commands generosity anyway.

This is precisely the point at which jubilee economics confronts the logic of pure self-interest and refuses it. The law knew that jubilee cut against the grain of ordinary economic calculation, and it commanded the harder thing anyway, because the purpose of the economy in God's vision is not the maximization of individual acquisition but the flourishing of the whole community, especially its weakest members. Jubilee subordinates efficiency to justice, incentive to mercy, the accumulation of the strong to the protection of the vulnerable. It is not that jubilee ignores the concerns of the prudent; it is that it ranks them below the concern for the poor, and it asks the prudent to accept a less optimized economy in exchange for one that will not permanently dispossess anyone. That trade-off is the whole argument, and where you land on it reveals what you believe an economy is finally for.

The jubilee will not be legislated back into a modern economy, and I am not calling for that. But its trumpet can still sound in the life of the church and the conscience of the believer. It sounds every time a debt is forgiven, every time the accumulated weight on a poor family is lifted, every time a Christian holds their property as a tenant of God rather than a lord of their own domain, every time a community shares so that none among it is destitute. The year of the Lord's favor has been proclaimed. Jesus said it was fulfilled in the hearing of those who listened. The only question is whether the church that bears his name will let the jubilee it announced reach as far as our own bank accounts, or whether we will keep insisting, against our own Lord, that the land is finally ours.

chapters.title: Read It Slower
chapters.summary: We have learned to read Scripture the way we read everything else. Fast, for information, to be done. That is not reading. It is scanning.
chapters.body:
"Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he meditates day and night." (Psalm 1:1-2)

We have forgotten how to read. Not the mechanics of it. The mechanics we do all day, faster than any generation before us, scrolling through more words by lunch than a medieval monk saw in a month. But that is not reading. It is scanning. It is extraction. We approach a page the way a machine approaches ore, to pull out the usable material and discard the rest, and we bring that same hunger to the Bible and wonder why it goes quiet on us.

The psalmist uses a different word. Meditates. And the Hebrew behind it, hagah, does not mean silent contemplation. It means to mutter, to murmur, to say the words half aloud over and over, the way a person chews something too tough to swallow whole. The blessed man does not consume the law. He ruminates on it. He turns one phrase over in his mouth for a day.

I confess I read Scripture fast for years. I read it the way I read a report, hunting for the point, eager to arrive at the takeaway so I could move on to the next thing. And it dried up in my hands. Not because the text failed. Because I was treating a feast like a memo. You cannot skim a well and expect to draw water.

So try the opposite. Take three verses, not three chapters. Read them once. Then read them again, slower. Then read them a third time and stop at the word that snags, the one your eye keeps returning to, and sit there. Ask why that word. Ask what it assumes. Ask what it would mean if it were true of you before noon. You will be amazed how much is in three verses that a hundred verses a day would have buried.

This is not a technique for the spiritually advanced. It is the recovery of something we lost. The people who wrote these words expected them to be read aloud, in a body, over a lifetime, the same passages returned to a thousand times, each return finding something the last one missed. The speed we bring to everything else is the one thing this book will not survive.

Slowness is not laziness here. It is reverence with a clock attached. It says this text is not raw material for my consumption but a living word I am invited to sit under. And a word you sit under long enough stops being something you read and becomes something that reads you.

Do not read more of it tomorrow. Read less of it, slower. Chew one verse until it gives up its water. Then swallow.

chapters.title: The Family Devotional Nobody Wants to Do
chapters.summary: For years our family devotions were a small nightly humiliation, and I was the one inflicting it, and I could not figure out why the thing I was sure was godly felt so much like a lie.
chapters.body:
For years our family devotions were a small nightly humiliation, and I was the one inflicting it. I would gather the boys, open the book, read the passage, ask the questions, and watch five sons perform varying degrees of endurance while I performed the role of the spiritual father. Someone would fidget. Someone would answer with the correct empty answer. Someone younger would ask when it would be over. And I would push through, because this was what a godly family did, and I could not figure out why the thing I was sure was righteous felt so much like a lie in the room.

It felt like a lie because it was one. Not the content. The content was true. The lie was in the theater, the performance of family worship that everyone was enduring and no one was receiving, the daily ritual whose real function had become allowing me to feel like a spiritual leader while my children learned to associate the Bible with boredom and dad's mild coercion. We were not worshiping. We were completing an assignment I had given us, and grading myself on whether we completed it.

The Guilt Machine

Almost every Christian parent I know carries guilt about family devotions. They are sure they should be doing them, sure they are doing them wrong or not enough, sure that other families have some serene candlelit thing they cannot achieve. The guilt is enormous and it is nearly universal and it produces two outcomes, both bad. Either the parents give up entirely and carry the guilt, or they grind out a joyless ritual and call it obedience while their kids quietly conclude that faith is a chore.

We have turned family worship into a performance that parents fail at and children endure, and then loaded the whole thing with guilt, and then wondered why our kids grow up thinking God is homework. We manufactured that association. It did not come from God.

Where did this guilt come from? Partly from a good instinct, the biblical command in Deuteronomy to teach these things to your children, to talk of them when you sit and when you walk and when you lie down and when you rise. But look closely at that command, because we have badly misread it, and the misreading is the source of the guilt. It does not prescribe a formal evening program with a workbook. It prescribes something both harder and easier, a whole life saturated with God, taught in the ordinary rhythm of the day. We took a command about the texture of a shared life and turned it into a scheduled event, and then felt guilty for failing at the event, which was never the command.

There is also a market that feeds the guilt, and I have contributed to it, so I say this as one of the guilty. A whole industry of family devotional products exists, each one implying that if you just had the right resource, the right format, the right curriculum, your family worship would finally become the glowing scene the cover photo promises. The guilt sells the product, and the product deepens the guilt when it too fails to produce the glowing scene, because the glowing scene was never real. It is a photograph, staged, with children who were bribed to sit still. Comparing your actual squirming family to that photograph is a game you were always going to lose, and the losing was the point, because a defeated parent buys the next book.

And there is a subtler layer of guilt underneath the product guilt, one that the market cannot reach because it is theological rather than commercial. It is the fear that if you do not run the program, God will hold it against you, that your children's souls hang on your consistency, that a missed devotion is a debt recorded somewhere against your account as a parent. This fear turns family worship into a work by which we try to earn God's approval or secure our children's salvation, which is precisely the opposite of the gospel we claim to be teaching. If the whole point of the faith is that we are saved by grace and not by our performance, then a devotional practice run out of terror of failing God is teaching our children the exact heresy the faith exists to overturn. God is not standing over your family with a checklist, docking points for the nights you were too exhausted to open the book. He is a Father, not an auditor, and a Father is far more interested in whether you know him than in whether you completed the assignment. The guilt is not from him. It never was. And a family devotion born of that guilt was always going to teach the wrong God.

What Deuteronomy Actually Describes

When you sit in your house, when you walk by the way, when you lie down, when you rise. That is not a devotional slot. That is every waking moment. The vision is not thirty formal minutes carved out of a day otherwise empty of God. The vision is a household where God is discussed in the car, at the meal, at the hard news, at the good news, in the argument, in the wonder, all day, informally, because he is genuinely part of the family's life and not a subject to be covered in a scheduled block.

The formal devotional was invented, in part, by parents trying to be obedient who reached for the tool they knew, the scheduled meeting, because our whole modern life is organized around scheduled meetings. But a scheduled meeting is precisely the wrong shape for what Deuteronomy describes. It concentrates all the God-talk into one dreaded slot and empties the rest of the day of it, which is the opposite of the command. The child in the joyless devotional is learning that God belongs in a box at 8 p.m. The command was that God belongs everywhere, all the time, in the flow of an ordinary day.

The Fix Is Not a Better Devotional

So the answer to the family devotional nobody wants to do is usually not a better devotional book or more discipline or more guilt. It is often to loosen the formal thing dramatically and to thicken the informal thing everywhere else. To stop measuring your faithfulness by whether you completed the evening program and start measuring it by whether God is a real, discussed, present part of your family's ordinary life.

The most spiritually formative thing in my house was never the devotional. It was the car. It was the dinner table when something hard happened. It was the moment a son asked a real question and I did not reach for the book, I just answered him, honestly, as his father.

This does not mean formal family worship is worthless. Rhythm and ritual have real power, and there is genuine value in the family that gathers to read Scripture and pray together, and I am not telling anyone to abandon it. I am telling you that if the formal thing has become a joyless performance that no one receives, the fix is probably not to double down on the performance. The fix is to make it shorter, simpler, more honest, and less frequent if necessary, while pouring your real energy into the all-day, informal saturation that the command actually describes. A five-minute reading and a genuine prayer beats a thirty-minute grind that everyone hates. And a spontaneous conversation about God in the car beats both.

Honesty in Front of the Children

What made my family devotions a lie was not the format. It was that I was performing a spirituality I did not feel in the moment, and my children could smell it. When I decided to stop performing, the whole thing changed. I started saying true things. I do not understand this passage either. This part of the Bible makes me uncomfortable. I have been struggling to pray lately. I got angry today and I was wrong. The devotional stopped being a performance of piety and became a place where a real man talked to his real sons about a real God he was really wrestling with.

That is what children need, and it is the one thing the workbook cannot provide. They do not need a father who has it all together dispensing tidy spiritual lessons. They need a father who is honestly following God, out loud, in front of them, stumbling included. The moment I let my devotions become honest instead of impressive, my sons started actually engaging, because now there was something real happening rather than a ritual being executed. Honesty is more formative than curriculum. It always was.

I remember the specific night this shifted. We had reached a hard passage, one of the ones about God's judgment that does not fit the tidy picture, and instead of smoothing it over with the answer from the study guide, I said, honestly, this one troubles me, I have never fully made peace with it, and here is what I hold onto anyway. And for the first time in years, a son leaned in. He had a question, a real one, not a performance of interest but genuine engagement, because for the first time the thing in the room was not a father performing certainty but a father actually thinking, in front of him, about a hard thing. That was worth more than every polished devotion I had ground out before it.

Let It Be Small

Here is permission that I wish someone had given me twenty years ago. Let it be small. A short Scripture and a real prayer at dinner is a family devotion. Talking about God in the car on the way to school is a family devotion. Praying together, briefly, when someone is scared or hurting is a family devotion. Pointing to God in a moment of beauty or grief as it happens is exactly what Deuteronomy commanded, and it counts, and it may count for more than the elaborate program you feel guilty for not sustaining.

The families whose children keep the faith are almost never the ones with the most impressive devotional systems. They are the ones where God was normal, discussed, present, real, woven through the ordinary hours in a way that made faith feel like the water the family swam in rather than a subject the family studied. You cannot manufacture that with a workbook. You grow it by living, out loud, as a person who actually knows God, in front of children who are always watching how you talk about him when you are not trying to teach them anything.

I want to guard this against a misreading, because the loosening I am describing can easily become an excuse for nothing. Letting go of the joyless formal program is not the same as letting go of God in the home. The temptation, once you drop the guilt, is to drift into a house where God is not discussed formally and also not discussed informally, where the loosening became simply an absence, and the children grew up with a father who was relieved of his devotional duty and never replaced it with anything at all. That is not the fix. The fix is not less God in the home. It is more God in the home, distributed differently, poured out of the artificial container and into the whole vessel of the ordinary day. If dropping the formal devotional means God comes up more, in the car and at the table and in the hard moments, then you have done the right thing. If it means God comes up less, or not at all, you have simply used my permission as cover for neglect, and your children will inherit not a living faith woven through the hours but a household where God was quietly retired. Loosen the form. Do not lose the God.

The Weight I Want to Leave

Drop the guilt. It was never from God, and it never produced anything but joyless performance and quiet resentment. The command was never that you run a flawless nightly program. The command was that God be real and present and discussed in your home, all day, in the ordinary rhythm of a shared life. That is harder in one way and infinitely easier in another, because it does not require you to be a curriculum expert. It requires you to be a person who genuinely follows God and does not hide it from your children.

If you want a place to start, start with your own honesty rather than a new curriculum. The next time something hard happens in your family, a diagnosis, a disappointment, a fear, do not manage it privately and present a calm face. Bring God into it out loud, in front of your children, in whatever words you actually have. God, we are scared, and we do not understand this, and we are trusting you anyway. That single sentence, spoken honestly at the right moment, will do more to teach your children how to walk with God through real life than a year of scheduled programs, because it shows them the thing itself, a person actually trusting God in an actual crisis, rather than a lesson about trusting God delivered in the abstract. Children do not need to be taught about faith nearly as much as they need to witness it, and they witness it most powerfully not in the devotional slot but in the moment the news is bad and they watch their parents turn toward God instead of away.

My family devotions got better the day I stopped trying to do family devotions and started trying to be a father who knew God out loud. Some nights we still open a book. Many nights we do not. But God is in the car, at the table, in the hard conversations and the good ones, all day, the way Moses said, and my sons grew up knowing him not as a subject we covered but as a Person we lived with. That was the assignment all along. I was just too busy grading myself on the wrong one to see it.

chapters.title: The Psalm for the Day You Cannot Fake It
chapters.summary: There is a day when the worship songs stick in your throat. Scripture wrote a prayer for that day and put it in the hymnbook.
chapters.body:
"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning?" (Psalm 22:1)

There is a day when you cannot fake it. You know the days I mean. The songs at church ask you to lift your hands and declare that God is good, and the words go dry in your mouth because at that moment you are not sure. The gap between what you are supposed to feel and what you actually feel has become a canyon, and standing in that room pretending it is not there is its own kind of exhaustion.

Most of us do one of two things with that day. We fake it, and add hypocrisy to the ache. Or we stay home, and add isolation to it. The church has quietly taught us these are the only options, that faith means summoning the right feeling or performing it convincingly, and that the absence of the feeling is a sin to be hidden.

Then you open the Psalms and find that God wrote a prayer for exactly that day and put it in the official hymnbook of his people. My God, my God, why have you forsaken me. That is not a private lament someone slipped in by accident. It is Psalm 22, sung by the congregation, canonized, kept. The Bible has a liturgy for the day you feel abandoned by God, and the liturgy does not scold you for feeling it. It hands you the words.

This is the thing the therapeutic version of faith cannot account for and the honest version depends on. Scripture does not require you to feel fine before you pray. It gives you a language for not being fine that is more honest than anything you would have dared to say on your own. Why are you so far. Where are you. Have you left. These are in the book. God preserved the accusation and called it Scripture.

And then, three hundred years before the cross, this psalm went where you are afraid to go and came out the other side. The same psalm that opens with abandonment turns, verse by verse, and by the end it is declaring that God has not despised the affliction of the afflicted, that all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord. It does not skip the darkness to get there. It walks straight through the middle of it. The praise at the end is not louder than the abandonment at the start. It is earned by having survived it.

Jesus prayed the first line of this psalm from the cross. He did not fake it either. In the worst hour, the Son of God reached for the words of a man who felt forsaken, because those words were true and he would not pray anything false, not even dying. If the sinless one prayed the psalm of abandonment, you are permitted to pray it too.

So on the day you cannot fake it, stop trying. Do not summon a feeling you do not have. Turn to Psalm 22 and pray the one that is already true. Ask the question the psalm asks. God is not going to flinch. He wrote the question into his own book and put it in the mouth of his own Son.

The day you cannot fake it is not the day faith ends. It may be the day it finally becomes honest.

chapters.title: The Verse You Have Read a Hundred Times
chapters.summary: The verse you can recite in your sleep is the one most likely to be dead to you. Familiarity is not understanding.
chapters.body:
"For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." (John 3:16)

You know this one. You could say it with your eyes closed. It was on the poster board at the football game and the bumper of the car in front of you and the wall of the Sunday school room where you first heard it. And that is exactly the problem. You have read it so many times that you no longer read it at all. Your eyes slide across it the way they slide across your own name.

Familiarity is not understanding. It is the counterfeit of understanding, and it is more dangerous because it feels like the real thing. I have quoted this verse from a pulpit and realized halfway through that I had not thought about a single word of it in years. I was reciting. I was not believing. The two can look identical from the outside.

So slow down and let one word catch. God gave. Not lent. Not offered on approval. Gave. The most costly thing in existence, handed over, and handed over to a world that John's own Gospel says did not receive him, did not know him, would nail him to a beam within the week. God so loved that world. The one that killed him. Read it as if you had never seen it, and it stops being a slogan and becomes a scandal.

Or catch the word whoever. There is no clause after it. No fine print, no membership requirement, no worthiness test. Whoever. It reaches down into every disqualification you have privately built for yourself, every reason you have decided the offer must have an exception with your name on it, and it refuses them all. Whoever means you, in the state you are actually in, not the state you keep promising to reach.

The tragedy of the famous verse is that we stop being surprised by it, and a gospel that no longer surprises us has stopped being good news and become mere information. Information does not save anyone. It sits in the mind like furniture. What saves is the moment the old verse cracks open and you hear it for the first time again, as if the ink were still wet.

Do not assume you have finished with the verses you have memorized. The memorizing may be the thing standing between you and them. Take the one you know best, the one you would never sit down to study because you already know it, and read it like a stranger. Let it be new. It has not changed. You have only stopped hearing it.

The verse is not tired. You are. Read it again.
